extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of theatre, actors, dramatists, and general readers interested in the theory and moral purpose of drama
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes normative criteria, qualities, and functions of dramatic art, actors, and fables as described in a literary/philosophical chapter on drama and the actor's apprenticeship. Useful for assessing plays, performances, and dramatic pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of dramatization: mimetic, child-creative, and fable
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatization of the savage is mimetic, 'a putting on from without of the disguise, the postures, sounds, motions, of the animal he impersonates.' The dramatization of the child is creative, 'a projection from within of his own thoughts and emotions into the counterfeit toys he personifies.' In fables these processes are joined with an inversion: the author 'puts his own human nature into the humbler creatures whom he dramatizes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to distinguish source and method of dramatic representation: whether action arises from external imitation, internal projection, or deliberate didactic inversion (fable). The differences affect intent, belief, and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fables: form and didactic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables are 'short compositions designed to teach moral truths, or to impress moral truisms, by representing beasts, birds, reptiles, insects, trees, flowers, or other objects, as endowed with the faculties of men, retaining their own forms but acting and talking as men, exemplifying the virtues and vices of men in characteristic deeds, followed by their proper consequences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating a fable, check for brevity, clear moral purpose, anthropomorphism that preserves animal form, exemplification of human virtues/vices, and a didactic outcome (consequence that illustrates the lesson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attractiveness of fables (fourfold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The attractiveness of fables is fourfold: (1) 'the incessant playing of human nature' in masks; (2) 'the congruous mixture ... of the most extravagant impossibilities and absurdities with the plainest facts and truths'; (3) 'the constant sense of superiority ... felt by the human auditor' over animal impersonators; (4) 'the interest and authority of the moral lessons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful fable typically combines dramatic play, imaginative impossibilities grounded by truth, an elicited empathic/comparative stance in the reader, and a vivid moral point. These four elements explain why audiences respond to fables and can be used as design criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre's purpose: hold up the mirror to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatre's business is 'to hold up the mirror to nature and humanity, that all styles of character and conduct may be seen in their proper quality and their true rank, teaching the spectators what to despise, what to admire, what to shun, what to imitate or reproduce for the perfecting of their own characters and conduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dramatic works by their capacity to present characters and conduct clearly and instructively so that audiences can form moral and aesthetic judgments. Theatre should make exemplars visible and legible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: instructional by contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy (the lower drama) exhibits 'inferior types of men and manners ... for the various purposes of amusement, ridicule, satire, correction.' Comedy teaches by 'opposition and contrast, showing what not to do and how not to do it, suggesting grace by awkwardness, hinting refinement by vulgarity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing comic drama, focus on its capacity to expose follies through contrast, to elicit corrective laughter or scorn, and to model better conduct indirectly. Effectiveness lies in apt contrasts and moral clarity rather than mere mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: higher drama to awaken admiration and moral reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy (the higher drama) represents 'superior social types ... to awaken admiration and reverence, to stir emulous and aspiring desires. Pity, love, and awe ... are moved and expanded.' It 'shadows forth the mysteries of fate and providence' and agitates 'insoluble problems of morality and religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tragic works by their ability to evoke deep passions (pity, awe, love), to present noble types worthy of emulation or reverent reflection, and to indirectly engage audiences with profound moral and existential questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodrama: intermediate spectacle and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Melodrama (the intermediate) 'brings forward a medley of characters, greater and lesser, good, bad, and indifferent, portraying life ... exaggeratedly, in heterogeneous combination' to give 'more than natural attraction for the senses' and provide 'strong sensations yet with small exaction on the mind.' Its business is to 'entertain and rest weary faculties with pleasurable amusement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess melodramatic pieces in terms of their sensory and pacing effects, their capacity to refresh and entertain without taxing cognitive faculties, and their structural use of exaggerated contrast. Recognize its legitimate role distinct from high moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and abuses of melodrama (legitimate vs illegitimate means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melodrama 'may be abused by the employment of illegitimate means, and thus perverted into an injury' — for example, 'pernicious in its exhibitions of nudity, impure postures, and prurient accessories.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge productions not only by their dramatic intent but by the means used: sensational or licentious devices that exploit audiences degrade artistic and moral value. The evaluator should weigh intent against methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational value of even petty or faulty plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a play is 'petty and worthless in plot ... full of absurdities ... pernicious,' two goods may be derived: (1) the sight of 'the superb power, grace, and skill of the trained performers' which serves as an exemplary model; (2) the melodrama's 'artistic groupings, colors, and movements ... draw our attention from ourselves, enlists our feelings in the fates of others, and thus exercising our faculties, disciplines, purifies, and emancipates them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poor dramatic works consider incidental benefits: exemplars of virtuoso performance and the disciplining/exercising effect on audience faculties. These can mitigate flaws in plot or morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of a great actor: mastery of inner states and sympathetic interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest actor 'is the one who is the most perfect master of all the signs of the inner states of men, and can in his own person exhibit those signs with the most vivid power.' He needs 'knowledge, the liberty, the spiritual energy and skill' and 'absence of prejudices and strictures, contracting ignorance and hate, and the presence of disinterested wisdom and openness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actors by their psychological insight, ability to internalize and convincingly express inner states, intellectual and spiritual openness, and moral seriousness. Mere external mimicry marks a charlatan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and technical requirements for actors
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor must 'have, to be completely equipped for his work, a mind and a body whose parallel faculties and organs are energetic and harmonic, every muscle of the one so liberated and elastic, every power of the other so freed and connected, that they can act either singly or in varied combination with others or with the whole, with easy precision and vigor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate physical training: flexibility, muscle control, precision, vocal strength, and the unity of mental and bodily faculties. Technical mastery of voice and gesture is a measurable criterion of professional worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and intellectual preparation: study, knowledge, and absence of charlatanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The first condition of truly profound and vital acting is to 'have the knowledge, the liberty, the spiritual energy and skill, to solve this inner side of the problem by reconstructing in the mind and heart the modes of character, passion, and conduct which are to be represented. They must be mastered and made one's own before they can be intelligently exhibited. It is the part of a charlatan to content himself with merely detecting and imitating the outer signs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate readiness by an actor's study of character, historical/cultural literacies, and depth of preparation. Superficial external imitation is a disqualifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship and humility: practical path to mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: A young actor should submit 'to a regular drill in the miscellaneous parts of the working stage, from top to bottom' and be 'willing now ... to take this humble position and hold himself ready for anything,' studying words' meanings and learning from mentors (Edwin's example of buying Walker's Dictionary and learning from Mrs. Riddle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When training or evaluating emerging actors prioritize breadth of stage experience, willingness to accept humble roles, rigorous study of text and pronunciation, and receptivity to instruction from seasoned performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama's moral function: cultivation of sympathy and reduction of cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic art is 'the exercise of that power whereby man can indefinitely multiply his personality and life, by identifying himself with others' and contributes to moral sympathy. Examples include extending sympathy to animals (prevention of cruelty societies) and the principle of Rarey: 'Free them from the spirit of opposition, and fill them with the spirit of obedient trust...' The development of sympathy 'tends to do for us what the doctrine of the transmigration of souls has done for the Hindoos.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drama partly by its capacity to enlarge sympathy, reduce cruelty, and foster moral imagination. Works that cultivate a broader sense of kinship and tender sentiment carry moral value beyond entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grades of histrionic inhabitation (states of acting)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 'five' grades given: the lowest is 'obsession' (man insanely held by inferior spirit), next 'sympathetic domination' (idea of another so seated it makes him involuntary agent), the intermediate 'voluntary assumption' (acting properly so called), 'inspiration' (loftier influences enhance and animate beyond volition), and lastly 'divine incarnation' (a deity deigns to inflesh and enshrine himself in man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hierarchy to conceptualize modes of performance and/or audience perception: from pathological or involuntary forms through deliberate craft to inspired or transcendent manifestations. It can guide both pedagogical aims (seek voluntary assumption and inspiration) and interpretative judgments.
